title: Ezekiel 7:1–13
context: The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel with a message for the land of Israel: “An end! The end has come on the four corners of the land” (7:2). The oracle repeats its themes like a drumbeat: the end, the day, the time, and the LORD judging the people according to their ways (7:3–9). The images of a rod that has blossomed and pride that has budded (7:10–11) are compact, and readers interpret them in more than one way. In 7:12–13 the ordinary business of buying and selling loses its meaning before the coming judgment. The notes name “the end has come” soberly, as the announcement of Jerusalem’s fall, without speculating beyond the text. Both traditions read the chapter as the climax of Ezekiel 4–7: the warnings given through signs and words are now declared certain.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel once more. Arminian readers see the prophet’s repeated reception of God’s word as showing the urgency of the message he must deliver.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that chapter 7 brings the sign-acts and oracles of chapters 4–6 to their climax. In common with Arminian readers, they hear what follows as the LORD’s own word, a final summons gathering up all the earlier warnings.

verses.text: “You, son of man, the Lord GOD says to the land of Israel, ‘An end! The end has come on the four corners of the land.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says to the land, An end! The end has come on the four corners of the land. Arminian readers see a decisive announcement that the time for warnings has run out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated end as a solemn declaration of God’s appointed judgment, compare Amos 8:2 by reference. Both traditions name the phrase soberly, as Jerusalem’s coming fall, reaching every part of the land.

verses.text: Now the end is on you, and I will send my anger on you, and will judge you according to your ways. I will bring on you all your abominations.
verses.arminianNotes: Now the end is on them; the LORD will send his anger and judge them according to their ways. Arminian readers stress the phrase according to your ways, as judgment corresponds to conduct.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s just measure, bringing their abominations back on them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as fitting judgment, in which the people meet the consequences of what they have done.

verses.text: My eye will not spare you, neither will I have pity; but I will bring your ways on you, and your abominations will be among you. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says his eye will not spare and he will have no pity, bringing their ways on them. Arminian readers note that this severity follows long patience and repeated warnings that went unheeded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the withdrawal of pity as God’s righteous decision when judgment’s time comes. Both traditions read the verse soberly, and they hold it alongside the remnant word in 6:8, without harmonizing the two.

verses.text: “The Lord GOD says: ‘A disaster! A unique disaster! Behold, it comes.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says, A disaster! A unique disaster! Behold, it comes. Arminian readers see the short, urgent exclamations conveying the shock of what is approaching.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that unique stresses the singular character of this disaster. Shared ground: both traditions read the staccato style as heightening the message’s urgency, and they do not try to rank this disaster against others.

verses.text: An end has come. The end has come! It awakes against you. Behold, it comes.
verses.arminianNotes: An end has come; it awakes against them. Arminian readers note the personification, as if the end itself rises up to meet the people, no longer delayed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the wordplay and repetition as hammering home the certainty of judgment. Both traditions read the verse as emphatic proclamation, carrying forward the announcement of 7:2 with growing intensity.

verses.text: Your doom has come to you, inhabitant of the land! The time has come! The day is near, a day of tumult, and not of joyful shouting, on the mountains.
verses.arminianNotes: Doom has come, the time has come, the day is near, a day of tumult, not joyful shouting on the mountains. Arminian readers see a reversal of the festivals once celebrated on the mountains.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the day as the day of the LORD’s judgment, a theme found across the prophets. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as turning celebration into tumult, and they hold the exact sense of doom loosely.

verses.text: Now I will shortly pour out my wrath on you, and accomplish my anger against you, and will judge you according to your ways. I will bring on you all your abominations.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will shortly pour out his wrath and judge them according to their ways. Arminian readers note the word shortly, stressing that the judgment is imminent, not distant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse repeating 7:3 to underscore God’s settled intent. Both traditions read the repetition as rhetorical emphasis, and they agree that the judgment is grounded in the people’s own abominations.

verses.text: My eye won’t spare, neither will I have pity. I will punish you according to your ways. Your abominations will be among you. Then you will know that I, the LORD, strike.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says his eye won’t spare, and they will know that he, the LORD, strikes. Arminian readers see the people recognizing that their calamity is not chance but the LORD’s response to their ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the variation, I, the LORD, strike, which names God as the agent of judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that history is not random, and that the LORD acts in justice.

verses.text: “ ‘Behold, the day! Behold, it comes! Your doom has gone out. The rod has blossomed. Pride has budded.
verses.arminianNotes: Behold, the day comes; the rod has blossomed and pride has budded. Arminian readers note that the rod may picture Babylon as God’s instrument, or Judah’s own pride grown to fullness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold more than one reading, some seeing the rod of judgment and others the arrogance of the people. Both traditions read the image as ripened readiness for judgment, and they leave its precise referent open.

verses.text: Violence has risen up into a rod of wickedness. None of them will remain, nor of their multitude, nor of their wealth. There will be nothing of value among them.
verses.arminianNotes: Violence has become a rod of wickedness, and nothing of their multitude or wealth will remain. Arminian readers see violence as the fruit that brings its own punishment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as stripping away every ground of security, people and possessions alike. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as showing that injustice and violence undermine the community from within.

verses.text: The time has come! The day draws near. Don’t let the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn; for wrath is on all its multitude.
verses.arminianNotes: The day draws near; the buyer should not rejoice nor the seller mourn, for wrath is on all. Arminian readers see ordinary transactions losing their meaning when judgment arrives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as relativizing earthly gain and loss before God’s judgment. Both traditions read the image as a sober reminder that possessions cannot shelter anyone from the day of the LORD.

verses.text: For the seller won’t return to that which is sold, although they are still alive; for the vision concerns the whole multitude of it. None will return. None will strengthen himself in the iniquity of his life.
verses.arminianNotes: The seller will not return to what was sold, for the vision concerns the whole multitude. Arminian readers note that the usual hope of reclaiming land, perhaps at a time of release, will fail in exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the vision’s sweep covering the whole people, with none strengthening themselves in iniquity. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the end of normal life in the land, and they hold any link to specific land laws lightly.
